meta.title: Teaching Binary With Coins

alignment_log.scope: Initial alignment pass: AP CSP, California K-12 CS Standards (6-8 and 9-12), CSTA 2017 (Level 2 and 3A).
alignment_log.note: 4 codes added, all strong or partial matches -- a single, focused lesson on binary/hex/RGB data representation lines up unusually cleanly with this specific slice of the data strand across every framework that has one. No explicit gaps recorded; nothing else in any catalog is close enough to be worth a checked:true entry for a one-page source this narrowly scoped.

meta.caveat: A single blog post, not a chaptered source -- locator_kind is "none" (so every entry shows just the post's own title, not "Unit post") and locator_url_template is the bare base_url with no {locator} substitution, since there's only one page to link to. Checked against CSTA 2026 too: that framework has no standard for binary/bit-level data representation at all (its own Data & Analysis strand is entirely data-science/spreadsheet-shaped, no binary-numbers equivalent survived from CSTA 2017 into the 2026 revision), so it's omitted outright rather than padded with a forced or checked-gap entry -- there's no code to even check against. CA CTE (ICT) does have a match (5.11) and is included below.

5.11.note: The anchor standard's own paraphrase, 'numbers can be represented in more than one base system, including binary and hexadecimal,' is close to a one-line summary of this whole lesson -- the coin-store base-2 conversion, then the byte-to-hex split in the last section.

2.1.note: The whole coin-store activity is this topic almost by definition: bits/bytes ('eight bits is a byte,' the 128-64-32-16-8-4-2-1 coin set), base-10-to-base-2 place-value conversion (the cash-register grid is DAT-1.C's algorithm, derived rather than handed over), and the two-agreements setup ('every amount from 1 through 15,' 'exactly one way') that pays off directly in the overflow discussion the post itself calls out ('what happens if you need 256 and only own eight coins,' DAT-1.B). EK DAT-1.A.6 ('combining bits... stand for higher-level things like numbers, letters, or colors') is close to a direct quote of the post's own RGB color-picker section.

9-12.DA.8.note: The color-picker demonstration (RGB, each channel 0-255) and the byte-to-hex conversion ('split a byte down the middle, convert each half, and you get two characters instead of eight') are this standard's own example set almost verbatim -- a color represented digitally in more than one way, converting between representations as a normal task.

6-8.DA.7.note: This carrier's own inference, mirroring 9-12.DA.8 above at the lighter 'representation changes what's easy to see' framing this 6-8 standard uses -- hex vs. binary for the same byte value is exactly that: which representation makes byte boundaries or bit patterns easier to read, which is the post's own argument for introducing hex at all.

3A-DA-09.note: Direct match: 'the same real-world thing... can be represented in more than one bit-level encoding, and you should be able to convert between them' is the byte-to-hex-to-RGB chain this lesson builds, explicitly named in the post's own 'AP CSP alignment' section (representing the same value multiple ways and explaining the choice).

2-DA-07.note: Even more literal than 3A-DA-09 above -- this MS-level standard names binary, an RGB value, and a hex code in one sentence, which is exactly the color-picker payoff: '#FFFFFF is white' by way of one byte, two hex digits, converted from binary and back.
